title: Neon only glows red-orange: every other colour in a ‘neon’ sign is a different trick

cover.alt: Colourful neon street signs glowing at night in Kabukichō, Shinjuku, Tokyo.

body: Pass several thousand volts through a glass tube of neon and the gas glows a distinctive reddish orange, the ‘blaze of crimson light’ that William Ramsay and Morris Travers saw when they discovered the element in 1898. Georges Claude turned it into advertising, showing two **12-metre** red neon tubes at the Paris Motor Show in December 1910 and selling two signs to Earle C. Anthony’s Packard dealership in Los Angeles in 1923. Every other colour needs a different recipe: mercury mixed with the neon gives blue, helium glows yellow or pink, and an argon–mercury mixture emits ultraviolet light that makes a phosphor coating inside the tube glow in almost any colour. Phosphors developed since the 1950s have added nearly 100 colours, so much of a ‘neon’ sign runs on something other than neon.

slides.heading: Match the gas to its glow
slides.explanation: Only the red-orange glow is neon itself. Argon–mercury tubes give off ultraviolet that makes a phosphor coating glow in almost any colour.

slides.label: the length of each red neon tube Georges Claude showed at the 1910 Paris Motor Show
slides.text: Neon sign tubes are blown from glass 9 to 25 mm across and run on several thousand volts.

slides.question: A tube in a sign glows blue. What is most likely inside?
slides.explanation: Blue comes from mercury: either mercury mixed with neon, or an argon–mercury mixture whose ultraviolet light makes a blue phosphor coating glow.
